newsitem.title: USA: San Francisco 49ers claim victory in stadium campaign.
newsitem.headline: San Francisco 49ers claim victory in stadium campaign.

text.p: Supporters of a $525 million football stadium-mall complex claimed victory on Wednesday after taking a narrow lead in San Francisco's hard-fought special election.

The two stadium measures on Tuesday's ballot had approval majorities of several hundred votes each, but city election officials said final results would not be known for several days because at least 4,500 ballots have yet to be counted.
Despite the slim margin, the San Francisco 49ers football team and their supporters declared victory. "49ers Win!!!" a campaign statement said.
Stadium opponents would not concede, saying the election was still too close to call. "We're optimistic," said Ellie Schafer, spokeswoman for the campaign against the stadium.

Voters narrowly approved Proposition D, which authorizes the sale of up to $100 million of bonds to finance the city's share of the stadium and shopping complex. They also backed Proposition F by the slimmest of margins, agreeing to waive stadium zoning restrictions to speed construction.

The vote capped a heated and sometimes bizarre stadium campaign that pitted San Francisco's flamboyant mayor, Willie Brown, against state Senator Quentin Kopp, one of the area's most powerful and outspoken lawmakers.
Stadium opponents had argued that the project was a form of "corporate welfare" because it would put San Francisco's budget on the line for the benefit of wealthy team owners.

Stadium supporters promised that the city would never have to dip into its general fund budget to pay off the bonds and told voters the project would create thousands of jobs for one of the city's poorest neighborhoods.

Brown said the bond deal would be structured by Morgan Stanley Group Inc. MS.N to protect city taxpayers and would include bond insurance by Financial Security Assurance, a unit of Financial Security Assurance Holdings Ltd..

Political analysts said they were somewhat surprised by the stadium's come-from-behind victory. Several had said the 49ers campaign lacked focus and failed to reach women voters. Recent voter polls suggested it would be soundly defeated.

In May, the stadium campaign was dealt its most serious blow when a raucous birthday bash for Jack Davis, one of San Francisco's most powerful political consultants who managed the campaign for the stadium, went public.
The private party, which featured live sex acts, strippers and sadomasochism, stunned one of the world's most tolerant cities and sent shockwaves through its political elite.
The controversy over the party, attended by many of the city's power brokers, snowballed, leading some to believe it could undermine public support for the stadium.

"They made mistakes," said political analyst Mark DiCamillo, director of the Field Institute in San Francisco, of the 49ers campaign. Turning it around on election day, he added, "was an amazing feat."
